      - run: python3 -m pip install coverage==7.16.1
      - run: python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/coverage -p 'test_*.py'
      - run: python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/release-hygiene -p 'test_*.py'
      # The adapters are only meaningful against the frameworks they adapt, so
      # CI installs them. Without them the suite still runs and skips those
      # cases, which would quietly assert nothing.
      - run: python3 -m pip install langchain-core==1.6.4 llama-index-core==0.14.25
      - run: python3 -B -m unittest discover -s sdk/python/tests -p 'test_*.py'
      - run: |
          unformatted=$(gofmt -l -s .)
          if [ -n "$unformatted" ]; then
            echo "::error::unformatted files:"
            echo "$unformatted"
            exit 1
          fi

  browser-smoke:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.2" }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version: "22" }
      - run: npm ci --prefix webui --ignore-scripts
      - run: npm exec --prefix webui -- playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: go build -o "$RUNNER_TEMP/entire-brain" ./cmd/entire-brain
      - name: Exercise the embedded UI in Chromium
        run: BRAIN_VIZ_BINARY="$RUNNER_TEMP/entire-brain" npm --prefix webui run test:browser
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: browser-smoke-traces
          path: webui/test-results/

  regression-mutations:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.2" }
      - name: Prove the selected tests catch their intended regressions
        run: python3 -B tools/coverage/mutation_check.py

  build:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    strategy:
      matrix:
        goos: [darwin, linux, windows]
        goarch: [amd64, arm64]
        exclude:
          - { goos: windows, goarch: arm64 }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.2" }
      - env:
          GOOS: ${{ matrix.goos }}
          GOARCH: ${{ matrix.goarch }}
        run: go build ./...

  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            runner: depot-ubuntu-24.04-8
          - os: macos-latest
            runner: depot-macos-26
    # The explicit name keeps matrix.runner out of the default display name:
    # "test (<os>)" is a required check on main.
    name: test (${{ matrix.os }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    # Backstop only. go test -timeout fires first and prints which tests were
    # still running, which is the useful artefact; neither job had any cap, so
    # a genuine hang ran to GitHub's 360-minute default.
    timeout-minutes: 45
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.2" }
      - name: Test with coverage and binary contracts
        run: python3 -B tools/coverage/run.py --race --output "${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage"
      - name: Retain coverage and test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-default-${{ matrix.os }}
          path: |
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.json
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.jsonl
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.out
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.html

  windows-test-prepare:
    name: test (windows-latest) / compile and plan
    runs-on: depot-windows-2025-8
    timeout-minutes: 30
    outputs:
      shard-matrix: ${{ steps.shard-matrix.outputs.value }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.2"
          cache-dependency-path: go.sum
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Validate the Windows sharding harness
        run: python -B -m unittest discover -s tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests -p "test_*.py" -v
      - name: Compile once and inventory default-runnable roots
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
          $repository = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '.').Path
          $output = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP 'windows-test-bundle'
          & python -B tools/ci-bench/windows-production/prepare.py `
            --repository $repository `
            --output $output `
            --settings tools/ci-bench/windows-production/settings.json `
            --weights tools/ci-bench/windows-production/historical-weights.json `
            --expected-repository-sha '${{ github.sha }}'
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit $LASTEXITCODE }
      - name: Export the authoritative shard matrix
        id: shard-matrix
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
          $planPath = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP 'windows-test-bundle/plan.json'
          $plan = Get-Content -LiteralPath $planPath -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
          $indexes = @($plan.shards | ForEach-Object { [int] $_.index })
          if ($indexes.Count -ne [int] $plan.shardCount -or $indexes.Count -eq 0) {
            throw 'plan shard indexes do not match shardCount'
          }
          $matrix = ConvertTo-Json -InputObject $indexes -Compress
          "value=$matrix" | Out-File -LiteralPath $env:GITHUB_OUTPUT -Encoding utf8 -Append
      - name: Upload immutable Windows test bundle
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: windows-test-bundle
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle
          if-no-files-found: error
          compression-level: 0
          retention-days: 3

  windows-test-shards:
    name: test (windows-latest) / shard ${{ matrix.shard }}
    needs: windows-test-prepare
    runs-on: depot-windows-2025-4
    timeout-minutes: 35
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      max-parallel: 8
      matrix:
        shard: ${{ fromJSON(needs.windows-test-prepare.outputs.shard-matrix) }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.2"
          # Shards execute precompiled binaries from the bundle; the module and
          # build caches this restores (~25s/shard) are never read.
          cache: false
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: windows-test-bundle
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle
      - name: Execute the assigned compiled roots
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
          $repository = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '.').Path
          $bundle = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle').Path
          $output = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP 'windows-test-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}'
          & python -B tools/ci-bench/windows-production/run_shard.py `
            --repository $repository `
            --bundle $bundle `
            --output $output `
            --shard-index '${{ matrix.shard }}' `
            --expected-repository-sha '${{ github.sha }}'
          exit $LASTEXITCODE
      - name: Upload shard evidence
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: windows-test-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 3

  windows-test-other:
    name: test (windows-latest) / non-heavy packages
    needs: windows-test-prepare
    runs-on: depot-windows-2025-4
    timeout-minutes: 40
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.2"
          cache-dependency-path: go.sum
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: windows-test-bundle
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle
      - name: Run every target-Windows non-heavy package once
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
          $repository = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '.').Path
          $bundle = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath '${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle').Path
          $output = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP 'windows-test-other'
          & python -B tools/ci-bench/windows-production/run_other.py `
            --repository $repository `
            --bundle $bundle `
            --output $output `
            --expected-repository-sha '${{ github.sha }}'
          exit $LASTEXITCODE
      - name: Measure instrumented CLI contracts without rerunning the suite
        run: python -B tools/coverage/run.py --race --binary-only --output "${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-other/binary-coverage"
      - name: Upload non-heavy package evidence
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: windows-test-other
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-other
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 3

  windows-test-vet:
    name: test (windows-latest) / vet
    runs-on: depot-windows-2025-4
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.2"
          cache-dependency-path: go.sum
      - run: go vet -race ./...

  windows-test-verify:
    name: test (windows-latest) / coverage and integrity
    needs: [windows-test-prepare, windows-test-shards, windows-test-other]
    if: ${{ always() && needs.windows-test-prepare.result == 'success' }}
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.2"
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: windows-test-bundle
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          pattern: windows-test-shard-*
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-shards
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: windows-test-other
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-other
      - name: Verify exact root, package, process, and artifact coverage
        run: |
          python -B tools/ci-bench/windows-production/verify_results.py \
            --bundle "${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-bundle" \
            --shard-results "${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-shards" \
            --other-results "${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-other" \
            --coverage-output "${{ runner.temp }}/windows-statement-coverage" \
            --output "${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-verification.json"
      - name: Render merged Windows statement coverage
        run: go tool cover -html="${{ runner.temp }}/windows-statement-coverage/combined.out" -o="${{ runner.temp }}/windows-statement-coverage/coverage.html"
      - name: Upload Windows statement coverage
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-windows-sharded
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-statement-coverage/
          if-no-files-found: warn
      - name: Upload verification report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: windows-test-verification
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-verification.json
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 3

  # Keep the former matrix check identity stable for required-check migration.
  windows-test:
    name: test (windows-latest)
    needs:
      [windows-test-prepare, windows-test-shards, windows-test-other, windows-test-vet, windows-test-verify]
    if: always()
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    steps:
      - name: Require every Windows test component
        env:
          PREPARE_RESULT: ${{ needs.windows-test-prepare.result }}
          SHARDS_RESULT: ${{ needs.windows-test-shards.result }}
          OTHER_RESULT: ${{ needs.windows-test-other.result }}
          VET_RESULT: ${{ needs.windows-test-vet.result }}
          VERIFY_RESULT: ${{ needs.windows-test-verify.result }}
        run: |
          for result in "$PREPARE_RESULT" "$SHARDS_RESULT" "$OTHER_RESULT" "$VET_RESULT" "$VERIFY_RESULT"; do
            if [ "$result" != success ]; then
              echo "A required Windows test component ended with: $result" >&2
              exit 1
            fi
          done

  # Discover every Python benchmark test module; Go tests do not cover the harness.
  benchmark-corpus:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    steps:
      # fetch-depth 0: the packet-format A/B modules assert that a recorded
      # product-contract commit is an ancestor of HEAD, which a depth-1 checkout
      # cannot answer.
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      # Evidence packaging uses tarfile's zstd support from Python 3.14.
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with: { python-version: "3.14" }
      # The task negative-control module drives the pinned Go toolchain. Same
      # story: the job had no Go at all.
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.26.2" }
      # That module discovers its toolchain with GOPROXY=off, deliberately — the
      # receipt it produces is only a negative control if the runtime is fixed
      # and local. So the pin it names has to be in the module cache before it
      # runs; this is the one command allowed to fetch it.
      - name: Prime the Go toolchain the task negative control pins
        run: GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.4 go version
      - name: Install Python coverage tracer
        run: python3 -m pip install coverage==7.16.1
      - name: Validate mined-scale corpus and run the benchmark test suite
        run: |
          set -e
          python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/mined-scale/check_manifest.py
          python3 -B -m unittest discover -s benchmarks/memory-ladder -p 'test_*.py'
          python3 -B tools/coverage/python_run.py --output "${{ runner.temp }}/python-coverage"
      - name: Retain Python coverage and module outcomes
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-python-benchmarks
          path: |
            ${{ runner.temp }}/python-coverage/*.json
            ${{ runner.temp }}/python-coverage/*.log
            ${{ runner.temp }}/python-coverage/html/

  benchmark-real-components:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with: { python-version: "3.14" }
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version-file: go.mod }
      - name: Check out the fixed Graph integration dependency
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          repository: entireio/entire-graph
          ref: b7511131319475860a935d2961b2b272429be4c7 # Graph main after PR #361: read-only store contract
          path: .integration-graph
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Build the real preparation components
        run: |
          go build -o "${{ runner.temp }}/entire-brain" ./cmd/entire-brain
          cd .integration-graph
          go build -o "${{ runner.temp }}/entire-graph" ./cmd/entire-graph
      - name: Exercise public benchmark preparation with local provider output
        env:
          ENTIRE_BENCHMARK_REQUIRE_COMPONENTS: "1"
          ENTIRE_BENCHMARK_BRAIN_BINARY: ${{ runner.temp }}/entire-brain
          ENTIRE_BENCHMARK_GRAPH_BINARY: ${{ runner.temp }}/entire-graph
        run: python3 -B benchmarks/agent-brain/test_full_brain_integration.py -v

I'm mapping out the full test.yml workflow—coverage runs on ubuntu/macos plus the windows job chain with prepare, shards, vet, and verify steps. For the selection PR, I'm noting that since cli sits atop nearly everything, selective testing only really pays off for changes isolated to tools/**, webui, benchmarks, and similar areas that don't touch cli.

Actually I need to reconsider: since cli imports almost every package, a change confined to one sub-package still forces cli's tests to rerun, so package-level selection can't skip the dominant cost unless it operates at a finer grain or cli itself gets smaller. That undercuts the promise that touching only one sub-package would demonstrably skip other packages' tests—since cli depends on everything, nothing above it gets skipped.

The real fix has to be structural: extract more logic out of cli so its suite shrinks to just command-assembly tests, making it cheap to always run, while selection logic stops rerunning untouched leaf packages. Given the user already agreed to this direction, I should go ahead and implement the selection mechanism now: compute affected packages via the reverse-import closure of changed files, run `go test -race` only on those (keeping a separate build job for compile checks across everything), push coverage profiling to post-merge/nightly runs instead of PR checks, and on Windows only run the heavier test shards when internal/cli is among the affected packages.

For merges to main, I'd keep the full run.py suite with coverage exactly as today so the required checks stay strict. Checking test.yml, I confirm run.py isn't invoked with --baseline there, so PR coverage is just informational, not a gate — meaning moving full coverage checks to main-push is low risk. This is exactly the kind of CI redesign COR-2268 calls for, but I want a conservative fail-safe: trigger a full suite run whenever certain sensitive paths change (go.mod/go.sum, tools/**, .github/**, build config, testdata, etc.), defaulting to full runs unless the change set is narrowly scoped to plain source files.

I also need to decide what happens with docs-only changes — should Go tests run at all, or should the job just pass trivially with an empty affected-package set? For computing affected packages, I'm leaning toward a small Python script that builds the reverse dependency closure from `go list -json ./...` output, mapping changed files to their containing packages via import path lookups, then using that in the test job to skip the run.py suite when nothing Go-related is affected.

Since internal/cli is affected by nearly every change and represents most of the test time anyway, a cleaner split is: PRs run `go test -race` against just the affected packages (no coverage instrumentation), while only main-branch pushes trigger the full coverage run.py. That keeps PRs fast without losing safety, since the common case of touching cli still gets exercised, and skips nothing when it matters.

For Windows, I want the harness selection to mirror this — skip the windows build/test chain entirely when the affected set doesn't touch internal/cli or other windows-relevant packages. A patterns-only change still reverse-depends on cli, so windows runs; docs or tooling-only changes can skip it. I'm tempted to keep windows unconditional for v1 since it's an 8-minute floor regardless, but conditionally skipping it for non-Go changes is still a meaningful win.

I'll bound v1 to just the test job: selection logic plus coverage for ubuntu/macos, moving coverage to run only on main-branch pushes, leaving windows and mutation/nightly jobs untouched for now. The test job stays required but conditions on event type — pull_request gets the fast no-coverage selected path, everything else runs the full suite — and I'll make sure the PR includes a demo showing skipped packages, since changing CI workflows is within scope here.

Since the lint job auto-discovers unittest files under tools/coverage and tools/release-hygiene, I'll place the new selector tool and its tests right there (tools/coverage/affected.py plus a matching test file) so it gets picked up automatically without needing a new discovery path. I'm now planning the affected.py tool itself — it'll take a base SHA and other inputs to determine...

For push/main, it stays full run.py unchanged, while PRs route through affected.py logic. The test_affected.py unit tests should use the real go list against the actual module rather than a fake graph, verifying known file-to-package mappings and reverse closures. On binary contracts, I'll keep them running always even in selected mode since they're cheap (~1 min) and worth the safety guarantee.

One tricky detail: checkout@v7 defaults to shallow depth=1, so git diff base...head needs either fetch-depth: 0 or a targeted shallow fetch of the base SHA. I'm leaning toward a narrow fetch of just the base commit at depth=1, then doing a tree-level diff between the two shallow refs instead of relying on merge-base, since full history fetch would add unnecessary CI time.

I'll implement PR selection via a new `tools/coverage/affected.py` that maps diffs to affected Go packages (running `go test -race` on just those, without coverage overhead), falling back to full coverage runs for non-.go changes or pushes to main. Windows CI stays untouched for now as a follow-up.

import json
import pathlib
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import unittest

TOOL = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "affected.py"
ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
MODULE = "github.com/entireio/entire-brain"


def run_tool(file_names):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".txt", delete=False) as handle:
        handle.write("\n".join(file_names) + "\n")
        listing = handle.name
    try:
        output = subprocess.check_output(
            [sys.executable, "-B", str(TOOL), "--changed-files", listing],
            cwd=ROOT,
            text=True,
        )
    finally:
        pathlib.Path(listing).unlink()
    return json.loads(output)


class AffectedSelectionTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_non_go_change_selects_the_full_suite(self):
        decision = run_tool(["tools/coverage/run.py"])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "full")

    def test_module_file_change_selects_the_full_suite(self):
        decision = run_tool(["go.mod"])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "full")

    def test_empty_change_set_selects_nothing(self):
        decision = run_tool([])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "none")

    def test_go_file_outside_every_package_selects_the_full_suite(self):
        decision = run_tool(["no/such/dir/x.go"])

All 7 selector tests pass, confirming the key semantics around test-import affectedness and cli-only changes excluding leaves. Now I'm wiring this into the test.yml workflow's test job, adding a step that fetches git history and runs the selector script to decide which packages are affected for pull requests.

I realize checkout@v7's default fetch-depth of 1 won't give me access to HEAD^1 on the merge commit, so I need to bump the test job's fetch-depth to 2 so the diff against the base tip works correctly; push events aren't affected since selection isn't used there. Then I'm adding a conditional test step that only runs when packages were selected, extracting the package list from the decision JSON and feeding them into `go test -race`, though I'm second-guessing the failure-forwarding approach and want to simplify it to a plain test invocation instead.

I also want to keep binary contract checks running cheaply on every PR via a race/binary-only run, while the full suite only runs on push or when the decision mode is "full" — with the "none" case (rare, empty diffs) possibly just echoing a no-op or still running contracts. I need to make the coverage artifact upload step conditional on whether the full-run actually executed, since otherwise upload-artifact will warn about missing files, and I'm also worried about referencing `fromJSON` on a skipped step's output when running on push events.

I'm reasoning through GitHub Actions' short-circuit behavior for `&&` in `if:` expressions — confirming that guarding with `github.event_name == 'pull_request' &&` before the `fromJSON(...)` call should prevent evaluating an empty string on push, since expressions short-circuit safely. As a more robust alternative, I'm considering having the affected-packages script output `mode` and a space-separated `packages` list as separate plain outputs instead of relying on JSON parsing in the workflow conditionals.

Now I'm restructuring the test job's steps: checking out the repo with enough fetch depth for diffing, setting up Go, then adding a "Select affected packages" step that only runs on pull requests, calls the affected.py script to write results to a temp file, prints it for debugging, and pipes the result into another script that writes mode/packages to the GitHub Actions output file.

After that, I'm adding conditional test steps -- one that runs race-detection tests on just the affected packages when mode is "selected", and another that measures instrumented CLI contracts via the coverage runner script when mode isn't "full".

Package names come from trusted `go list` output, so no injection risk there. On PR events the checkout grabs the merge commit, which only exists if the PR is conflict-free, and both ubuntu and macos test jobs stay as required checks while the selection logic just speeds them up — setup-go runs before affected.py so the module's ready, and macos has python3 available too.

steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          # Depth 2 exposes the PR merge commit's first parent (the base tip),
          # which package selection diffs against. Pushes ignore the extra depth.
          fetch-depth: 2
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.2" }
      # Pull requests run only the packages the diff can affect (reverse import
      # closure, including test imports) with -race and WITHOUT coverage
      # profiling: -coverprofile disables Go's test caching and adds atomic
      # counter overhead, and PR coverage artifacts were informational only.
      # Any non-.go change falls back to the full coverage run below. Pushes to
      # main always run the complete coverage suite, so merged evidence is
      # unchanged.
      - name: Select affected packages (pull requests)
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        id: affected
        run: |
          python3 -B tools/coverage/affected.py --base HEAD^1 --head HEAD > "$RUNNER_TEMP/affected.json"
          cat "$RUNNER_TEMP/affected.json"
          python3 -B -c '
          import json, sys
          decision = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
          print("mode=" + decision["mode"])
          print("packages=" + " ".join(decision.get("packages", [])))
          ' "$RUNNER_TEMP/affected.json" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - name: Test affected packages with race
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && steps.affected.outputs.mode == 'selected'
        run: go test -race -count=1 -timeout 30m ${{ steps.affected.outputs.packages }}
      - name: Measure instrumented CLI contracts without the full suite
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && steps.affected.outputs.mode != 'full'
        run: python3 -B tools/coverage/run.py --race --binary-only --output "${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage"
      - name: Test with coverage and binary contracts
        if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' || steps.affected.outputs.mode == 'full'
        run: python3 -B tools/coverage/run.py --race --output "${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage"
      - name: Retain coverage and test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-default-${{ matrix.os }}
          path: |
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.json
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.jsonl
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.out
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.html

**Draft [PR #518](https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/518) is up — the CI selection step**, the direct answer to your question.

How it works after this merges:
- A PR touching only `internal/cli/patterns` runs patterns + its importers (4 packages), not the whole suite.
- A PR touching only core `cli` skips all the extracted leaf packages and drops coverage instrumentation (~10–20% CPU).
- A docs/tools/workflow change, or anything the selector can't prove safe, falls back to today's full coverage run. Pushes to main are completely unchanged — full coverage evidence continues there.
- The selection semantics are pinned by 7 unit tests that run against the real module graph in the existing lint job on every CI run.

1. **`TestRefreshAnnouncesAutoSelectedAgentOnStderr` executes the real `codex` binary** when installed (the seed agent phase uses raw `exec`, bypassing the fake runner) — ~69 seconds of actual agent run per local suite execution, and the likely cause of the recorded "local suite times out" baseline. Fast on CI only because codex isn't installed there. Deserves a small test-isolation fix.
2. The old "semantic is heavy" assumption is dead — remaining weight is refresh/transcript ingestion, and much of it is root-command integration that extraction alone won't relocate.

CI watcher armed — note this PR's own run deliberately exercises the fail-safe full path (it changes `.yml`/`.py`); the first Go-only PR after merge will demonstrate the selected path.

def changed_files(base, head, cwd=ROOT):
    # --no-renames keeps a rename visible as an add plus a delete, so a .go
    # file moved between packages marks BOTH packages as changed. With rename
    # detection, --name-only lists only the destination and the source package
    # would silently keep its stale selection.
    output = subprocess.check_output(
        ["git", "diff", "--name-only", "--no-renames", f"{base}", f"{head}"],
        cwd=cwd,
        text=True,
    )
    return [line for line in output.splitlines() if line.strip()]

import json
import pathlib
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import unittest

TOOL = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "affected.py"
ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
MODULE = "github.com/entireio/entire-brain"


def run_tool(file_names):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".txt", delete=False) as handle:
        handle.write("\n".join(file_names) + "\n")
        listing = handle.name
    try:
        output = subprocess.check_output(
            [sys.executable, "-B", str(TOOL), "--changed-files", listing],
            cwd=ROOT,
            text=True,
        )
    finally:
        pathlib.Path(listing).unlink()
    return json.loads(output)


class AffectedSelectionTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_non_go_change_selects_the_full_suite(self):
        decision = run_tool(["tools/coverage/run.py"])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "full")

    def test_module_file_change_selects_the_full_suite(self):
        decision = run_tool(["go.mod"])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "full")

    def test_empty_change_set_selects_nothing(self):
        decision = run_tool([])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "none")

    def test_go_file_outside_every_package_selects_the_full_suite(self):
        decision = run_tool(["no/such/dir/x.go"])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "full")

    def test_leaf_package_change_includes_its_importers(self):
        decision = run_tool(["internal/cli/patterns/corpus_access.go"])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "selected")
        packages = set(decision["packages"])
        self.assertIn(MODULE + "/internal/cli/patterns", packages)
        # cli imports patterns, and the main module wires the cli root command,
        # so both must re-run when patterns changes.
        self.assertIn(MODULE + "/internal/cli", packages)

    def test_top_package_change_excludes_packages_it_does_not_reach(self):
        decision = run_tool(["internal/cli/root.go"])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "selected")
        packages = set(decision["packages"])
        self.assertIn(MODULE + "/internal/cli", packages)
        # Nothing in cli is imported by the leaf helper packages, so a cli-only
        # change must not re-run them.
        self.assertNotIn(MODULE + "/internal/cli/patterns", packages)
        self.assertNotIn(MODULE + "/internal/cli/internal/base", packages)

    def test_test_only_dependency_affects_its_test_importers(self):
        decision = run_tool(["internal/cli/internal/clitest/clitest.go"])
        self.assertEqual(decision["mode"], "selected")
        packages = set(decision["packages"])
        # clitest is imported only by _test.go files; test imports must still
        # count as affectedness or moved pins would silently stop re-running.
        self.assertIn(MODULE + "/internal/cli", packages)
        self.assertIn(MODULE + "/internal/cli/patterns", packages)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

git push -u origin cor-2268-isolate-agent-exec 2>&1 | tail -1 && gh pr create --base main --title "test(cli): stop fixture refreshes from executing the real agent binary" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Why

While measuring remaining CLI test weight for [COR-2268](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2268), the single heaviest test turned out to be `TestRefreshAnnouncesAutoSelectedAgentOnStderr` at ~69s locally — because it was **executing the real `codex` binary**. Agent *resolution* goes through the fake `CommandRunner`, but the seed synthesis phases run the resolved agent as a real subprocess (deliberately — agents are real programs). On a developer machine with codex installed, every suite run silently invoked the real agent with real agent-side spend; CI never saw it because no agent is installed there. This is the dominant single cost in the local suite and a likely cause of the recorded local-timeout baseline.

## What changes

A test helper, `isolateRealAgentBinaries`, prepends PATH shims for `codex`/`claude` that exit 1 immediately — pinning every machine to the exact CI behavior (the synthesis phase fails fast; refresh tolerates it and continues). Applied to the two full-refresh fixture tests that resolve an agent.

- `TestRefreshAnnouncesAutoSelectedAgentOnStderr`: ~69s → **0.48s** (race)
- `TestRefreshAnnouncesPinnedModel`: ~3.1s → 0.42s
- Assertions unchanged; inventory unchanged (3479 roots); Windows no-ops (no agent installed there, and absent binaries already fail instantly).

## Note

This is the first Go-only PR after #518, so its CI run also demonstrates the new affected-package selection path: the `test (ubuntu/macos)` jobs should show `mode=selected` with `cmd/entire-brain internal/cli` and skip the extracted leaf packages.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

content.thinking:
This one has 9 subtests across scopes and variants, each building real git fixtures and running actual subprocesses plus export — legitimate integration work worth the ~2s, not something to speed up. I'd previously rejected sharing mutable fixture state across these tests since it risks flakiness, so I'll skip this one too — no more easy single-test wins remain.

Looking at what's left, two paths stand out: narrowing Windows CI jobs by affected packages to cut the ~8 min floor for leaf-only PRs, or continuing extraction work on the refresh/transcript subsystem. Since ubuntu/macos are already down to ~3.5-4 min while Windows still runs everything regardless of what changed, selective Windows chain execution gives the biggest win per PR right now. I'm scoping out how windows-test-prepare could run affected.py first, skip compiling the cli test binary and shards when internal/cli isn't affected, while still satisfying the required-check identity — making the shards job matrix conditional and having run_other select only the affected non-heavy packages.

I'm aware this requires verify_results.py to understand reduced-scope plans exactly, since it currently asserts full coverage against the plan — so the harness itself (settings/contract tests, fail-closed logic) needs updating, which is the sensitive part. A simpler v1: when cli is unaffected, skip the compile+shards step but still run non-heavy jobs on whatever Windows-specific packages were touched, since Windows path/lock semantics matter for leaf packages too — and teach verify to accept that reduced plan. It's a chunky, risk-concentrated change to the harness, but given the session budget and merge cadence, I want to proceed carefully, starting with reading through prepare.py's heavy-vs-other split and the run_other logic.

But stepping back — how often is cli actually unaffected by a Go PR? Since base/brainstore/patterns/workspace/entities all get imported transitively into cli, almost every package change ends up affecting it. Only a handful of leaf packages (factmerge, agentsetup, apiurl, maybe brainwire) wouldn't touch cli, so this Windows-skip optimization would rarely trigger today — its real payoff only shows up once commands are decoupled from cli's current import-everything topology, which is a much longer-term restructuring, not something achievable in this PR.

So the only wins available right now are shrinking the cli suite's own runtime (currently 147s on CI, within a 3m23s job) or accepting there's little else low-hanging. The real bottleneck is the ~8 minute Windows floor, dominated by compile (~3 min) plus shards (~4-5 min) — and since cli is always affected, I can't skip it, only make it leaner by extracting packages so the -race compile and test work shrink. That only helps if the extracted tests move to the non-heavy job that runs in parallel with the shards, rather than just producing more recompilation inside cli.

Given that, the real lever is continued extraction of test weight — refresh/transcript, brief, workspace commands, history — which was already my planned next step before this detour into shard rebalancing. With plenty of token budget left and each extraction taking roughly 1-2 hours of focused work, I'll start scoping the refresh/transcript boundary now, aiming to carve out a bounded PR that extracts the transcript store and canonical ingestion layer.

Looking closer though, much of the fileless test weight is root-level export/refresh integration tests that stay tightly coupled to the root package, similar to what happened with workspace. So the extraction mainly shrinks compile units rather than actually relocating tests — the returns are diminishing. Given I've just hit a natural milestone with selection working end-to-end, the right move is to report status honestly, flag where the remaining wins actually are, and let the user decide how much further investment makes sense here.

I want to check the acceptance criteria for COR-2268 against where things stand now — comparing current CI timing (leaf-PR path, test job durations) against the original baseline of roughly 8.2 minutes for the Windows chain plus 4 minutes for test jobs, to see how much of the promised speedup is actually realized.

The honest picture: selection works and shipped, but every Go PR still pulls in the cli importer suite, which runs ~147s, plus the Windows chain at roughly 8 minutes. Further gains would require extracting integration-heavy subsystems, which is a grindier effort with diminishing returns — so this feels like a real decision point to surface to the user rather than just pushing ahead autonomously. I should update the Linear ticket with the as-built state and acceptance status, then let them choose whether to continue extraction work or stop here and bank the wins.

content.text:
#519 validated on merged main (the fixed tests run in 2.8s under race). I also checked the two remaining ~20-second singles before continuing — and the finding changes the picture, so here's an honest status before I commit us to the next grind:

**Both remaining heavy singles are legitimate.** The mcp-deadline test must build a store slow enough to observe a mid-build deadline firing (that's the regression it pins); the fileless test is 9 real git-fixture export runs (and fixture sharing was explicitly rejected in a recorded decision as flake-prone). No more cheap wins of the #519 kind.

**Where CI time actually stands now:**
- ubuntu/macos PR jobs: ~3.5–4 min, of which `internal/cli` is 147s. Since `cli` imports every extracted package, **every Go PR still runs the cli suite** — selection skips the leaves, but the giant always runs.
- Windows chain: still the ~8-minute floor (compile ~3 min + shards ~4–5 min), and Windows selection would almost never fire today for the same reason — everything affects cli.

**What this means for the remaining COR-2268 roadmap:** the only lever left for the per-PR floor is continuing to shrink `cli` itself — and the measurement shows what remains in it is mostly root-command integration weight (refresh/export/brief flows), which the workspace experience showed relocates poorly: implementations move, but the root-command tests stay. Further extractions still pay off (smaller Windows `-race` compile, shard weight moving to the parallel non-heavy job, more cache isolation), but each PR now buys less than the ones already landed.

**My recommendation:** before the next extraction, spend one cheap step updating the Linear ticket with the as-built state and acceptance measurement — what landed (9 PRs: #503→#519), the demonstrated selection run, current per-PR timings vs the original ~8.2-minute floor, and the revised cost/benefit of the remaining candidates (refresh/transcript, brief, history, Windows-floor work). That gives you a clean decision point on how much more to invest versus banking the wins.

Want me to write that ticket update (and the Brain record), or push straight on into the refresh/transcript extraction?

{"id":"COR-2268","uuid":"a0097fbe-c0bf-48c8-a984-49193ad512bf","title":"Split entire-brain internal/cli into sub-packages so Go's test cache and package parallelism work","description":"## Why

`internal/cli` is one Go package with \~3,450 top-level tests (\~1,700 test roots). This single-package shape defeats two Go mechanisms CI would otherwise get for free:

* **Test caching**: any one-line change in `internal/cli` invalidates and re-runs the entire suite on ubuntu, macOS, and all Windows shards. With 6–8 packages, a PR touching one area re-runs a fraction.
* **Package-level parallelism**: `go test` runs packages concurrently but tests within a package serially unless each test opts in. We hand-added `t.Parallel()` to 84 tests (entire-brain#470), but \~19 more are stuck serial because their fixtures isolate via `t.Setenv` (process env) — package boundaries parallelize without that audit.

It is also why the Windows CI needs its bespoke 8-shard harness: one package cannot be split across runners by `go test`, so `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/` compiles once and deals individual test roots to shard runners, one process per root.

Current numbers (after entire-brain#469/#470/#475): `test (ubuntu/macos)` ≈ 4.0 min each, Windows chain (prepare → shards → verify) ≈ 8.2 min = the run's wall-clock floor.

## Suggested boundaries

By measured test time and name clustering (largest first): `mcp` (\~172 tests), `workspace` (\~141), `pattern` (\~112), manifest/seed (\~71), `distill` (\~136), `history` (\~135), `semantic` (\~254), `brief` (\~118), remaining core. Boundaries can differ — the goal is 6–8 packages of comparable test weight, not these exact nine.

## Coupling the implementer must handle

* **Windows harness**: `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/settings.json` names `./internal/cli` as the only heavy package and pins its `TestMain` declarations by file name + AST SHA-256 (`expectedTestMainDeclarations`). `historical-weights.json` keys per-test weights by import path. Both must be updated per new package (or non-cli heavy packages added to the heavy list); `verify_results.py` requires an exact root partition and will fail closed on drift.
* **Workflow contract tests**: `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests/test_workflow_contract.py` pins workflow structure; update alongside.
* **Coverage harness**: `tools/coverage/run.py` runs `./...` with `-race` — should be unaffected, but `tools/coverage/mutation_check.py` cases in `mutations.json` reference packages/tests by path.
* **Nightly**: `.github/workflows/nightly.yml` windows-verify compiles `./internal/cli` as one `cli.test.exe` and runs it directly (detached-worker file-lock workaround, documented inline) — becomes N binaries or a loop.
* **Scale-mode helper**: `internal/cli/scale_mode_test.go` (`ENTIRE_BRAIN_OBSERVED_SCALE`, set by nightly) gates fixture sizes for tests in `brain_manifest_read_test.go` / `seed_manifest_scale_test.go`; it must move with (or be duplicated into) whichever package gets those tests.
* Tests swap package-level hooks (`memoryWorkerLaunch`, `beforePatternCorpusPublish`, `maxManifestBytes`, `defaultMaxReadBytes`, …). Splitting forces these seams to become exported or injected — that is most of the real work, and also the opportunity to fix the known detached-worker leak (tests exercising the real `memoryWorkerLaunch` re-exec the test binary as `cli.test memory worker --once` children that outlive the suite; see entire-brain#470 discussion).

## Acceptance

* `internal/cli` split into 6–8 packages of roughly comparable test weight; `go test ./...` green with `-race` on all three OSes.
* A PR touching only one sub-package demonstrably skips the others' tests via Go's test cache (or via per-package CI selection).
* Windows shard plan covers the new packages exactly once each (verify job green).
* No test weakened: same assertions, same fixtures, moved not rewritten.","priority":{"value":0,"name":"No input.body:
## Status: selection is live; extraction continues to have value but with thinner returns

### What landed (2026-10-25 → 2026-10-26)

Twelve PRs, all merged, full race suite green on every one:

- **Foundations**: #486 (base + clitest + entities pilot), #490 (workspace storage/graph), #492/#494/#496/#498/#500/#501 (patterns, brainstore locks/reads/snapshots, corpus publication/access).
- **Privacy layer**: #503 (session privacy state → brainstore), #507 (read guard, retrieval policy locking → brainstore; derived-read gate → patterns, verifier injected).
- **Unfreezing**: #510 (`main_test.go` TestMain delegates to `clitest.PinXDGRoots`; harness hash updated — the one deliberate `tools/ci-bench` change), #515 (env/XDG/store-path resolution → base).
- **Payoff**: #516 (workspace pattern corpus + families → patterns, including all six heavy family integration tests; 10 roots moved). #517 cleanup.
- **CI selection**: #518 — PRs run only diff-affected packages (reverse import closure incl. test imports) with `-race` and no coverage; non-Go changes fail safe to the full coverage run; pushes to main unchanged.
- **#519**: fixture refreshes were executing the real `codex` binary on dev machines (~69s per suite run, real agent spend; invisible on CI where no agent is installed). Fixed with fail-fast PATH shims; 69s → 0.5s. Likely the cause of the long-standing "local cli suite times out" baseline.

### Acceptance status

- "PR touching one sub-package demonstrably skips the others" — **met**, demonstrated live: #519's CI run selected `{cmd/entire-brain, internal/cli}` and skipped every extracted package. ubuntu test job 3m23s (was ~4.0–4.4m).
- "green with -race on all three OSes" — **holds** on every PR; Windows verify green throughout, shard plan covers moved roots correctly (weights fall back by design).
- "tests moved not rewritten" — **held**: every moved root byte-compared under a mechanical rename map; inventories reconciled exactly on every PR (currently 3,479 cli / 32 patterns / 34 brainstore / 18 base / others).
- "6–8 packages of comparable test weight" — **not met**: cli still holds ~97% of roots. See below for why the original target needs revisiting.

### What the fresh measurement changed

Full `-race` per-test timing at current main (3,444 roots, 561s elapsed sum):

- The ticket's suggested boundaries no longer match the weight. `semantic` (~254 tests suggested) is now 130 roots at **9.7s**. The heavy groups are refresh/ingestion (86s — but 69s of that was the #519 agent-exec bug, now gone), transcript-fileless (47s), remaining workspace commands (41s), brief (25s).
- The remaining heavy tests are mostly **root-command integration** (full `refresh`/export runs over real git fixtures) plus two legitimate singles (mcp deadline-observation 20s, fileless export matrix 19s). The workspace extraction showed this class does not relocate: implementations move, root-command tests stay in cli.
- Because cli imports every extracted package, **every Go PR still re-runs the cli suite (147s on CI)**. Selection pays off fully only for the leaf packages, and the Windows ~8-minute floor is untouched by selection for the same reason.

### Remaining options, by value

1. **Keep extracting** (refresh/transcript store, brief, history): shrinks cli's compile unit (helps the Windows `-race` compile, the recorded wall-clock hog) and moves what unit-level weight exists, but the per-PR gain per extraction is now smaller than the landed ones.
2. **Windows chain selection**: low value until the import topology changes — cli is affected by almost every Go change.
3. **Root-command test cost**: the remaining big wins would come from cheaper integration fixtures or splitting command assembly itself (cli stops being the universal importer). Larger design change; not in the original ticket scope.

Recommend deciding explicitly how much of 1–3 to fund before scheduling further extraction PRs.

content.text:
Posted the status update to [COR-2268](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2268) and recorded it in Brain.

The comment covers, for a cold reader:
- **What landed**: the twelve merged PRs (#486 → #519), grouped by arc — foundations, privacy layer, the main_test.go unfreeze, the workspace-pattern payoff, CI selection, and the real-agent-execution fix.
- **Acceptance scorecard**: selection demonstrated live and race-green everywhere with moved-not-rewritten held; the "6–8 balanced packages" criterion explicitly marked not met (cli still ~97% of roots).
- **What the fresh measurement changed**: the ticket's original boundary suggestions are stale (semantic is now light), the remaining weight is root-command integration that extraction doesn't relocate, and — the structural point — cli imports everything, so every Go PR still pays the 147s cli suite and the ~8-minute Windows floor is selection-immune.
- **The three remaining options ranked by value**, ending with an explicit ask to decide funding before more extraction PRs get scheduled.

That closes the loop on this work session: everything merged is validated on main, the ticket reflects reality, and the next move is a scoping decision rather than more code.

content.text:
Honest answer: **partially — the mechanism is real and proven live, but the magnitude is limited by the repo's shape.**

**What you actually got:**
- On #519 (a one-file test change), CI genuinely ran only 2 packages instead of the whole module — the log shows `{"mode": "selected", "packages": [cmd/entire-brain, internal/cli]}` and every extracted package (patterns, brainstore, workspace, entities, base…) was skipped, coverage instrumentation dropped. The ubuntu test job went from the historical ~4.0–4.4 min to **3m23s**.
- Locally the win is bigger: extracted packages now cache across runs, and the suite no longer secretly executes the real `codex` agent (~70s + real API spend per run, fixed in #519).

**What you didn't get — and why:** I just probed four true leaf packages (`factmerge`, `apiurl`, `brainwire`, `agentsetup`), and every one of their reverse-import closures **still contains `internal/cli`** — because cli imports essentially everything to assemble the root command. So there is currently *no possible Go change* that skips the cli suite, and the cli suite is 147s of the job. Likewise the Windows chain (~8 min, the real floor) compiles and shards cli on every PR regardless of selection.

So the before/after for a typical small Go change:

| | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| ubuntu/macos test job | ~4.0–4.4 min (everything + coverage) | ~3.4–4.1 min (cli closure only, no coverage) |
| Extracted packages | always re-run | **skipped unless touched** |
| Windows chain | ~8 min | ~8 min (unchanged) |
| Local full suite | timeouts, real agent runs | ~70s faster, hermetic |

The remaining gap is structural, not mechanical: as long as `internal/cli` is both 97% of the tests and the universal importer, every change pays it. Closing that gap means either continuing to move test weight out of cli (diminishing per-PR returns, as the measurement showed) or the bigger step the original ticket didn't scope — splitting command assembly so cli stops being one giant package that imports the world. That's the decision now sitting in the Linear comment.

content.thinking:
I'm thinking through what "splitting command assembly" would mean concretely for this repo — right now internal/cli bundles root command setup, every individual command's implementation, and all their tests into a single package, with cmd/entire-brain/main.go simply calling cli.NewRootCommand() to wire it all together.

Splitting it means moving each feature's command constructor, run logic, and tests into its own subpackage (like refreshcmd or briefcmd), leaving the root cli package as a thin assembler that just mounts each command onto cobra. That way, a change to one feature only touches its own package plus the nearly test-free root assembler, so CI only needs to run that feature's tests instead of the whole cli package — turning minutes-long test runs into seconds, since the "universal importer" at the root no longer drags in everyone else's tests.

The hard part is honest to assess: today's commands cross-call each other's unexported helpers (refresh calling seed, workspace touching patterns, shared retrieval logic across get/brief/mcp), so each shared helper needs a new home, which is the bottom-up work we've been doing but now at scale. Shared test fixtures need to move into a clitest-style package too, and the trickiest bit is the root-level integration tests that invoke the full command tree — some genuinely test cross-command behavior and belong with the assembler, while others should be repointed at the individual feature's own cobra command, which means deciding where to relax the "moved-not-rewritten" rule.

Beyond that, mcp.go acts as a hub touching nearly every feature so it either needs interfaces or stays big, and the Windows test harness's per-package pinning or sharding may need retiring once packages are small enough. Effort-wise this is comparable to or larger than everything done so far since the prior PRs only moved a small fraction of the root, but it's now more mechanical given the foundations in place, and each command cluster can be its own bounded PR — matching the original ticket's vision of a handful of packages, with the groundwork already built. The payoff: isolated test runs per command, parallel compiles on Windows, and eventual retirement of the heavy shard harness. I want to lay this out readably with a small diagram, just explaining rather than acting, and close with what a pilot slice would look like.

content.text:
Today, `internal/cli` is really two things fused into one package:

```
cmd/entire-brain ──> internal/cli ──────────────> patterns, workspace, entities,
                     │                            brainstore, base, …
                     ├─ NewRootCommand()          (the extracted leaves)
                     ├─ refresh: command + implementation + tests
                     ├─ brief:   command + implementation + tests
                     ├─ privacy, seed, mcp, viz, dash, get, …
                     └─ 3,479 test roots
```

The **assembly** (building the cobra root, mounting subcommands, wiring `Options`) and the **feature implementations** live in the same package. That's why cli is simultaneously 97% of the tests *and* in every package's reverse-import closure — any change anywhere re-runs it.

**Splitting command assembly** means inverting the top of that graph:

```
cmd/entire-brain ──> internal/cli (thin assembler, ~zero tests)
                        ├──> refreshcmd.New(opts)   + refresh tests
                        ├──> briefcmd.New(opts)     + brief tests
                        ├──> privacycmd.New(opts)   + privacy tests
                        ├──> workspacecmd.New(opts) + workspace command tests
                        └──> …
                     each of those ──> patterns / brainstore / base / …
```

Each feature package exports its own cobra command constructor; the root package just imports them and mounts them. The crucial consequence: the universal importer still exists, but it's **nearly test-free** — so being in every closure costs nothing. A change to brief re-runs `briefcmd` (~25s of tests) plus an empty assembler, not 147 seconds of everything. Windows stops having one giant `-race` compile unit, and the bespoke 8-shard harness can likely shrink toward plain per-package `go test`.

This is actually what the original ticket sketched ("6–8 packages: mcp, workspace, distill, brief…"); the twelve PRs so far built the basement that makes it possible (shared helpers, privacy gates, env resolution, test pins all have importable homes now).

**Why it's the expensive option — the honest costs:**

1. **Cross-command calls.** Commands reach into each other's internals today (refresh runs seed, workspace calls pattern surfaces, get/brief/mcp share the retrieval pipeline). Every shared helper needs a home package — same discipline as the last twelve PRs, but applied to the remaining 97%.
2. **`mcp.go` is a second hub** — it calls across nearly every feature. It either becomes its own big package (fine) or needs interfaces.
3. **The moved-not-rewritten rule bends slightly.** Root-integration tests that run `cmd.SetArgs(["refresh", …])` through the full root would re-point at `refreshcmd.New(...)` instead of `NewRootCommand(...)` — a one-line, principled change, but a change; a small set of genuinely cross-command tests stays with the assembler.
4. **Windows harness per package** — heavy-list entries and TestMain pins per new package, or a deliberate decision to retire sharding once no package is heavy. We've already done this dance once (#510), so it's known territory.

Rough shape if you fund it: one pilot PR per command cluster, starting with the most self-contained one (brief or viz) to validate the recipe, then the heavy ones (refresh/export, workspace commands, mcp) — probably 6–10 PRs of the same size as the recent ones. End state is the actual dream: a one-command change runs that command's tests in seconds, on every OS.

No action needed from me now — happy to scope the pilot (exact first cluster, its closure, and what the re-pointed tests look like) whenever you've thought it over.

I need to give a real recommendation on whether the command-assembly split is worth it, grounded in the actual numbers rather than a generic survey. Weighing costs: roughly 6-9 PRs of similar size and effort, likely 1-2 weeks of this working style, with moderate risk since the moves are mostly mechanical and already have a solid verification recipe proven across 12 prior PRs—except for the shared retrieval piece, which is the one genuinely tricky spot.

On the benefit side, today's CI pays a steep tax—roughly 8 minutes per PR including the Windows floor—while a properly split architecture could cut that to 3-4 minutes for typical changes, since per-command builds would run in seconds and the heavy Windows compile unit would shrink dramatically. Given the repo's PR volume (around 10-20 per day), that adds up to meaningful savings in both CI compute and human wait time, and the local dev loop benefit—running tests on a single small package in seconds instead of waiting on a 10+ minute build—may be the bigger win overall.

Retiring the bespoke CI harness also removes a standing maintenance tax that bit us during #510, and as a bonus it unblocks the Windows test selection option. My honest take is this is worth doing, but as an incremental background effort rather than a big rewrite: start with a cheap single-package pilot (brief or viz) to get real numbers before committing further.

I want to frame the justification around the compounding wins — local dev loop speed and killing the Windows harness — rather than CI minutes alone, and keep my final answer concise and opinionated with the actual measurements included.

content.text:
Yes — with one qualifier about how to buy it.

**The case for:** the payoff isn't just CI minutes, it's three compounding things:

1. **The per-PR floor actually falls.** Typical change today: ~4 min ubuntu/macos + ~8 min Windows, every time. After the split, a one-command change runs that command's package (seconds–30s) plus a near-empty assembler; and Windows' real cost — the ~3-minute `-race` compile of one giant package plus 6 shards — dissolves into medium packages that plain `go test` can parallelize. Plausible end state is ~3–4 min total, mostly fixed overhead. At this repo's PR velocity (I count ~20 merged PRs this weekend), that's hours of wall-clock and compute weekly, forever.
2. **The local dev loop is the bigger win.** Right now touching brief means re-running a 10+ minute package locally (the recorded "local suite times out" baseline, and until yesterday it also secretly ran a real agent). After the split it's `go test ./internal/cli/briefcmd` in seconds. That's friction every engineer pays daily.
3. **You get to delete the Windows sharding harness.** `tools/ci-bench` is a bespoke, fail-closed system that taxes every structural change (we paid that tax in #510). Once no package is "heavy," it retires. Deleting maintained machinery is worth more than the minutes.

**The case against is mostly gone.** The MCP removal killed the second hub; the twelve landed PRs already built the hard substrate (shared helpers, privacy seams, env resolution, test pins all have homes); the verification recipe (inventory reconciliation, normalized body comparison, race gates) is proven and catches loss. The genuinely uncertain part is one area: the shared retrieval pipeline behind `get`/`brief`, plus the judgment calls on re-pointing root-integration tests.

**The qualifier:** don't commit to all ~6–9 PRs up front. Fund **one pilot** — `viz` or `brief`, the most self-contained cluster — as a single PR. It validates the recipe on the new shape (command constructor, re-pointed tests, Windows handling) and gives you a measured number for what a per-command package actually costs and saves. If the pilot's numbers look like the projection, the rest is mechanical and can proceed at whatever pace suits; if the retrieval coupling turns out nastier than expected, you've spent one PR learning that instead of six.

So: worth it, pilot-first, and I'd pick `brief` as the pilot since it also carries real test weight (25s) that moves on day one.

Yes, this matches how major Go CLIs are structured — kubectl and Docker CLI both use a thin root command that assembles subcommands living in their own packages, confirming this is the idiomatic pattern for large CLI tools.

t (package get) is the pattern, so I'd suggest internal/cli/command/refresh or internal/cmd/refresh, naming the package after the feature without a redundant "cmd" stutter — kubectl's pkg/cmd/get follows this convention too, and the Options/Factory injection mirrors gh's cmdutil.Factory approach. I should also note that our internal/cli/internal/base nesting, while unusual, is legal and fine, and keep the final answer concise with concrete exemplars.

content.text:
Yes — it's not just idiomatic, it's the standard shape for every large Go CLI you'd name as a reference:

- **The Go toolchain itself**: `cmd/go/internal/{build,get,mod,run,test,...}` — each subcommand is its own internal package exposing a `*base.Command`, and `cmd/go/main.go` is a thin assembler that just registers them. This is the canonical example.
- **GitHub's `gh`**: `pkg/cmd/{pr,issue,repo,...}`, each package exporting `NewCmdPR(f *cmdutil.Factory)` with its own tests beside it; the `Factory` struct injects IO, config, and clients — almost exactly our `Options{Env, Runner, Now}` pattern, which means the dependency-injection style we've already built is the one this structure expects.
- **kubectl**: `pkg/cmd/{get,apply,delete,...}`, one package per command, assembled in `pkg/cmd/cmd.go`.
- **Docker CLI**: `cli/command/{container,image,network,...}`.

The current shape — one giant package holding every command plus its implementation — is the counter-pattern. Terraform's `internal/command` is the big-package example in the wild, and it suffers exactly the symptoms this ticket opened with (huge compile unit, no package-level test parallelism or caching).

Two idiom notes for the pilot, if it happens:

1. **Naming**: Go style prefers short, lower-case package names without stutter. The exemplars use a `cmd`/`command` parent directory with the feature as the package name — so `internal/cli/command/brief` (package `brief`) reads better than `briefcmd`. Since we already use `internal/cli/...` as the tree, something like `internal/cli/command/{brief,refresh,workspace,...}` fits what exists.
2. **What we already have is the unusual part, and it's fine**: the double-internal (`internal/cli/internal/base`) is legal and does its job (helpers invisible outside the cli tree), but it's rarer in the wild than a flat `internal/{base,brainstore,...}`. Not worth churning now — just don't deepen it further.

So structurally, the split moves the repo *toward* ecosystem norms, not away from them. The only non-idiomatic risk would be overdoing injection — `gh`'s Factory works because it stays small; if a command package ever needs a 15-field deps struct, that's a sign the helper belongs in a shared package instead.

# Entire repository agent guide — Graph and Brain

Use Brain for task context, retained knowledge, and history.
ALWAYS check Brain availability and version once per session, at the first
substantive task or historical question, BEFORE the brief or any fallback:

    entire brain version
    entire brain capabilities --json

Validate the version output and structured capability report, not just the exit
status. Confirm the required features are supported; use command help when the
report does not identify a required command. Record the version, supported
capabilities, and an available, missing, or unsupported result for the session.
A dev version is not evidence of an outdated binary; check its capabilities.
EVERY tool-unavailability fallback MUST trace to this recorded check and be
explained to the user. Capabilities do not prove repository readiness: record
later query failures or missing-index evidence separately, and limit each
fallback to the affected question. Never defer the preflight until a query fails.

ALWAYS begin a substantive task with:

    entire brain brief "<task>" --json

Run the brief before substantive source exploration or implementation.
Familiarity with the repository, supplied file paths, and remembered context
do not waive this requirement. Specs, reviews, and refactoring plans count
as substantive tasks.

Previous decisions, rationale, prior attempts, documentation, durable project
memories, and earlier sessions MUST be investigated with Brain first, ALWAYS.
Knowing what the current code does does not establish why it was written.
Do not substitute recollection, source comments, or a plausible explanation
for retrieval of the recorded evidence.

Retrieve prior decisions, rejected approaches and rationale with recall, not
with query and not from the brief's memories sample alone:

    entire brain recall "<question>" --json

Use Brain retrieval for recorded knowledge. Use entities history when connecting
code changes to earlier checkpoints or sessions. ALWAYS retrieve relevant prior
decisions and attempts before proposing to replace an existing approach.
ALWAYS consult relevant retained knowledge when reviewing a change.
A general brief does not replace targeted retrieval for a historical question
that the brief did not answer.

Cite the retrieved evidence for historical claims. Distinguish recorded rationale
from inference. An empty result means no evidence was found; it does not establish
that a decision or previous attempt never existed.

Durable memories are Brain's episodic record. When you establish something durable
that the code does not already state - a decision and its rationale, an
invariant, a gotcha that cost you time - RECORD it before finishing:

    entire brain remember "<memory>" --path <category.subcategory.type> --json

Categories are architecture, constraints, preferences, project and workflow.
Omitting --path classifies the memory for you and requires a supported coding
agent on PATH; pass --path when none is guaranteed. Retrieve with recall and
re-check anchors with verify. A memory you author has no source anchor, so verify
reports it unverifiable-here - that is expected, not a failure.

Brain semantic answers refer to a stored index, which may differ from current
working-tree source. Verify claims about present behavior against current source
and executed tests.

Use Graph for code discovery, structural understanding, and semantic change analysis.
ALWAYS check Graph availability and version once per session, at the first
structural question or code discovery task, BEFORE querying or using a fallback:

    entire graph version --json
    entire graph capabilities --json

Validate the output, not just the exit status: version must identify the
entire-graph provider, and capabilities must report the features and semantic

content.thinking:
The user wants the command-assembly split done with each command as its own package, using sub-agents and a project trail with sub-trails — a big undertaking I need to plan carefully, starting with the brain brief and figuring out whether this counts as a new session needing a fresh graph preflight.

For the trail structure, I need to figure out how parent/sub-trail relationships work — checking the trail create help or the MCP tool for that support, since the user wants one project trail with multiple sub-trails underneath.

Then comes the actual technical plan: enumerating the commands in root.go, grouping them into clusters that each become their own internal/cli/command package with a constructor, migrating files and tests, extracting shared helpers where needed, and sequencing the work so self-contained clusters go first.

But I'm realizing there's a serious risk to running sub-agents in parallel here — they'd all be touching the same cli package and root.go, and since every extraction renames call sites and moves shared helpers, overlapping edits from multiple agents on the same files would create merge conflicts. That's presumably why the prior PRs for this were done sequentially rather than in parallel.

So the safer approach is a sequential first phase where I personally set up the trail, scope out the clusters, map the shared-helper dependencies like the retrieval pipeline, and write a clear package layout and recipe doc so each sub-agent has a complete brief to work from. Then in a second phase, isolated worktree-based agents could tackle near-disjoint clusters in parallel, accepting that each will still need to touch root.go to remove its own command block — small, mechanical conflicts I can resolve with rebasing.

Realistically, I'll kick off two or three agents on the most independent clusters and merge them in sequentially rather than all at once. Each cluster's PR still needs to pass the full verification battery — inventory reconciliation, the race suite, and the Windows harness — though since the heavy list only names the cli package specifically, new standalone packages should automatically fall into the non-heavy category, and as cli shrinks the shard weights should rebalance fine.

Given the scope of this, I see my role as orchestrator: set up the plan and trail structure, dispatch worktree-isolated sub-agents with detailed briefs per cluster, verify what comes back, and land things sequentially. Starting with some quick preflight checks on brain/graph versioning and capabilities, then a brain brief and recall pass to firm up the command structure decisions.

From there I need to inventory the full command surface in root.go, design the cluster list with ordering and a landing protocol, create the project trail plus sub-trails, write up the recipe doc in .context for the sub-agents to follow, and then dispatch the first wave. Starting with the preflight and command inventory now.

content.thinking:
I'm cataloging the full set of roughly 45 commands and thinking about how to group them into natural clusters based on their coupling, since splitting each into its own package would be unwieldy — each cluster would become its own sub-trail or PR, starting with the most self-contained ones like version, capabilities, path, doctor, and config.

Beyond that, I'm laying out heavier clusters: viz, dash, the setup cluster, lifecycle/ingestion commands, workspace, patterns, the facts cluster, distill, the shared retrieval surface (get/query/search/etc.), memory/privacy, semantic repair/inspect, publish, and stats/docs/benchmark. That lands around 12-14 clusters total, and the key complication is that many commands share underlying implementation — the retrieval pipeline, storage resolution helpers, and output-writing utilities — so the recipe for each cluster needs to account for what gets reused versus extracted fresh.

I'm now sizing each cluster against the scale of a prior reference PR, which suggests 12-14 similarly-sized efforts, each needing command files to move along with their run functions while shared internals keep sinking into internal packages. With sub-agents handling mechanical work and me verifying and landing, it's a long haul but doable since the user gave the go-ahead.

I'm thinking through orchestration: one branchless project trail describing the overall plan, with sub-trails per cluster PR that attach automatically when their branch starts. I'm trying to recall whether trails support parent-child linking, since the user wants one project trail with as many sub-trails as needed, and I remember seeing a "Project trail" link shown earlier that suggests this structure already exists.

I'm reviewing the trail creation flags available and noticing there's no explicit parent option, so linking will likely happen through referencing sub-trails in the project trail's body text rather than a formal hierarchy -- I plan to create the branchless project trail first, let each cluster branch auto-generate its own trail on push, then update the project trail body with links, checking the help output to confirm there's no parent support before finalizing this approach. I also want to draft a recipe document capturing the per-cluster verification steps, naming rules, and landing protocol so sub-agents have clear guidance to follow.

For dispatch, I'm planning wave 1 as 2-3 parallel agents in worktrees tackling the most independent clusters, with sequential landing and rebasing as needed afterward -- conflict risk is mostly contained to root.go edits (removing old command references and moving files), since different clusters otherwise touch separate files, so tight scope per agent should keep parallel work safe. Since sub-agents won't share my context, the recipe doc needs to be thorough, and I should also brief them on worktree isolation practices.

Actually, simpler plan: agents work in worktrees and commit their work, then I cherry-pick/rebase onto main sequentially, run full gates, push, and open a PR per cluster. Rather than dispatching all clusters at once, I'll start with a pilot wave of 2 (viz and misc/meta) to validate the approach before scaling up to more waves, while I prepare the closures for wave 2 in the meantime. First though, I want to check whether trail create already supports parent/sub relationships.

For the file closures, I need to map out which files belong to each cluster — checking where webui gets embedded relative to viz.go, and gathering the files/dependencies for the misc/meta commands (version, capabilities, path, doctor). I'll do quick greps to confirm these closures, noting that for simple command constructors like newVizCommand, the only caller is root.go, which is trivially verifiable. The sub-agents themselves will need to run their own graph impact checks as part of their briefs.

Preflight checks are done (Brain v0.3.0-17 and Graph v0.6.0 both available), and I've compiled the full command inventory (~45 commands across 8 groups). Next I'll set up the project trail and shared recipe, starting with a check on trail parenting support and the wave-1 cluster closures.
